reader.summary: During the week of October 24 to November 1, 2026, Israel held its first parliamentary election since the October 7 attacks, producing no clear winner. Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc edged ahead of Gadi Eisenkot's opposition camp but fell short of a majority, while Palestinian Arab parties posted record turnout and emerged as decisive kingmakers in coalition talks. Netanyahu immediately alleged the vote was stolen by foreign entities and pushed for probes into the Arab sector; the opposition accused him of delegitimising the result. President Herzog urged both sides to form a government rather than trigger a new election, and weeks of coalition haggling began. In the West Bank, the Israeli military carried out a major operation in Hebron, demolishing homes and displacing thousands of Palestinians around the vote. In Gaza, Israel launched its first strikes since May, killing a Hamas commander, though a ceasefire was also reported to hold. In Serbia, an assailant was shot dead outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade. The shekel and Israeli bonds fell on the uncertainty, and Iran's supreme leader warned the US and Israel against resuming war. A Swiss court upheld complaints that TV commentary on Israel's Olympic bobsleigh team was discriminatory.

key_events.event: Israel's Knesset election produced no clear winner; Netanyahu's bloc leads but lacks a majority, and Arab parties become kingmakers.
Netanyahu claims the election was stolen by foreign entities and pushes for probes into the Arab voting sector.
Israel carries out a major military operation in Hebron, demolishing Palestinian homes and displacing thousands ahead of and during the election.
Israel launches its first targeted strikes in Gaza since May, killing a Hamas commander, while a ceasefire is also reported to hold.
President Herzog urges both Netanyahu and Eisenkot to form a government rather than call a new election.
An assailant attacks a police officer outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade, Serbia, and is shot dead.
Iran's supreme leader warns the US and Israel against resuming war, as reports say the two are planning a new strike on Iran.
Israeli bonds and the shekel fall as the inconclusive election leaves both camps short of a parliamentary majority.
A Swiss court upholds complaints that TV commentary on Israel's Olympic bobsleigh team was discriminatory.
The Netherlands withdraws from Eurovision over Israel sensitivities, and 36 countries are confirmed for Eurovision 2027.

plain.summary: Over the coming week, Israel's political crisis will dominate the news cycle. Netanyahu will push a formal Knesset motion to recount Arab-sector ballots, and Eisenkot's camp will respond with sharp denunciations. President Herzog will press both sides to negotiate, but the gap between them will widen. In the West Bank, the Hebron operation will expand, with more homes demolished and thousands more Palestinians displaced, drawing fresh UN warnings. In Gaza, the ceasefire will hold in name but Israel will carry out at least one more targeted strike, and rockets will land near Tel Aviv. The shekel will stay under pressure as markets wait for clarity on who will form the government. The Swiss bobsleigh ruling and the Eurovision withdrawal will fade from the headlines. A small chance exists that Eisenkot and the Arab parties strike a preliminary deal, which would upend the entire coalition calculus and force Netanyahu into a defensive posture.

crystal.summary: Israel will be defined next week by the grinding coalition negotiations that follow its inconclusive election. Netanyahu and Eisenkot will trade public attacks and competing policy offers as they race to court the Arab parties whose record turnout made them kingmakers. President Herzog will press both sides to form a government before the deadline for a second election looms. In the West Bank, the Hebron operation will press on with further demolitions and displacement, drawing fresh criticism from the UN and the opposition. In Gaza, the ceasefire will hold in broad terms, but Israel will carry out additional targeted strikes against Hamas, keeping the truce fragile. The shekel and bonds will stay volatile as markets digest the political uncertainty. The overall tone will be one of a country in limbo, where no one governs and everyone argues.

Netanyahu and Eisenkot will each pursue separate tracks of coalition talks with Arab party leaders, while President Herzog pressures both camps to avoid a second election. Netanyahu will press his fraud narrative, and the Interior Ministry will open a formal probe into voting in Arab-majority districts, giving Arab parties a new chip in their kingmaker leverage. In Gaza, the fragile ceasefire will face its first stress test as Israel responds to the killing of a Hamas commander with further strikes, and rockets will land near Tel Aviv. The shekel and bond markets will react to each round of political news. The Swiss bobsleigh ruling will fade. A surprise Supreme Court petition from Netanyahu to review the election result will add legal uncertainty to the political deadlock, and the question of a second vote will loom over every headline.

display.headline: Israel's Coalition Race Heats Up as Arab Parties Hold the Keys
emoji_reasons: The election result and its aftermath dominate the entire political landscape
Coalition formation and government-building are the central question of the week
Military operations in Hebron and targeted strikes in Gaza keep the security front active
display.tldr: Israel will spend the week in a coalition scramble, with Netanyahu and Eisenkot competing for Arab party support while the president urges a deal. Hebron demolitions will press on and Gaza's ceasefire will hold but stay fragile. Markets will stay jumpy.
display.eli5:
Israel just had a big election and nobody won clearly. Netanyahu's side got the most seats but not enough to rule alone, and the Arab parties that voted in record numbers now hold the keys to who gets to form the government.

The reason this is a mess is that both Netanyahu and his rival Eisenkot need the same small Arab parties to join their coalition, so they're both trying to sweet-talk them while also bashing each other on TV.

Next week you'll probably see a lot of coalition horse-trading in the headlines, with both sides making offers and the president trying to keep them from calling another election. You'll also see more news about the military operation in Hebron, where homes are being torn down and families are being moved out.

A surprise would be if the two camps suddenly agree to a joint government, or if a big rocket attack or security incident happens and changes who gets the moral high ground in the talks.
